items.title: What Emotional Intelligence Is — Concept & Origins
items.body:
### What Emotional Intelligence is, and where it came from

**The idea in one sentence**
Emotional intelligence is the skill of noticing and managing your own feelings, and of reading and responding well to other people's feelings, so that emotion helps your decisions instead of hijacking them.

**Do it the slow way first (reason through a scenario)**
Imagine two officers receive the same rude email from a colleague.
1. Officer A feels the anger, notices it ("I am angry because this felt disrespectful"), waits ten minutes, then replies with plain facts.
2. Officer B feels the same anger and fires back at once with a sharp reply; the quarrel grows and the real work stalls.
Both officers are equally clever and hold the same degrees, so raw reasoning power (IQ) did not separate them. What separated them was that A recognised the feeling, paused, and chose a response, while B was ruled by the feeling. That difference — noticing, understanding and managing emotion, in yourself and in others — is exactly what "emotional intelligence" names. Working through it slowly (feel the emotion, then notice it, then name it, then choose the action) also shows the key exam point: EI is a habit that can be learned and strengthened with practice, unlike IQ, which stays roughly fixed through life.

**What the symbols mean (the key terms)**
There are no maths symbols here; these are the terms the exam tests.

| Term | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| EI / EQ | emotional intelligence / emotional quotient — the same idea |
| IQ | intelligence quotient — cognitive, analytical reasoning ability |
| ability model | EI treated purely as mental skills, measured by performance tests |
| mixed model | EI treated as abilities blended with personality traits and habits |

**The formula or method**
The exam's favourite origins question is "who did what, and when". Fix it as a short timeline you can recite: **Salovey and Mayer coined the term in 1990 → Goleman popularised it in his 1995 book → Bar-On built the EQ-i self-report test and spread the word "EQ".** Keep "coined" and "popularised" apart — this single distinction answers most history questions.

**Exam-level example**
"The term 'emotional intelligence' was first coined in a 1990 paper, and later made popular by a 1995 bestseller. The two who coined it, and the one who popularised it, are:" The correct pairing is Salovey and Mayer (coined, 1990) and Goleman (popularised, 1995). Gardner (multiple intelligences) and Thorndike (social intelligence) are earlier influences but did not coin the term; Bar-On built a test but did not coin it either. Check it against the timeline above and it holds.

**Common traps**
- Saying Goleman "coined" EI — he only popularised it (1995); Salovey and Mayer coined it (1990).
- Treating EI as the same as IQ — IQ is stable and cognitive; EI is developable and emotional-social.
- Thinking EI means hiding or suppressing emotion — it means using emotion wisely, not deleting it.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Salovey and Mayer, 1990 | coined the term "emotional intelligence" |
| Goleman, 1995 book | made it famous ("may matter more than IQ") |
| Bar-On, EQ-i | mixed/trait test; spread the word "EQ" |
| EI is learnable, IQ is stable | you can train emotional skill |
keyPoints: EI = recognising, understanding and managing one's own emotions and responding well to others' emotions.
Salovey and Mayer coined 'emotional intelligence' in 1990; Goleman popularised it in his 1995 book.
Bar-On built the EQ-i mixed/trait test and spread the term 'EQ' (emotional quotient).
IQ is cognitive and roughly fixed; EI is emotional-social and can be developed with practice.
Goleman's claim: for leadership, EI can matter more than IQ.
items.source: Salovey & Mayer (1990); Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); Britannica — Emotional Intelligence

items.title: Goleman's Five Components of EI
items.body:
### Goleman's five components of EI

**The idea in one sentence**
Goleman splits emotional intelligence into five everyday skills — three about managing yourself (self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation) and two about managing relationships (empathy, social skills).

**Do it the slow way first (reason through a scenario)**
Follow one officer through a tense morning and label each skill as it appears.
1. He feels his chest tighten in a meeting and thinks, "I am getting defensive." That noticing is **self-awareness**.
2. He wants to snap back but takes a breath and answers calmly instead. Holding the impulse is **self-regulation**.
3. The meeting goes badly, yet he stays set on finishing the project well. That drive despite a setback is **motivation**.
4. Later a junior seems quiet and low; he senses she is upset before she says so. Reading her feeling is **empathy**.
5. He brings two quarrelling teammates together and gets them cooperating again. Managing that relationship is **social skills**.
Notice the order is not random: he had to *notice* the feeling (1) before he could *control* it (2). The three self-skills come first because you cannot handle other people's emotions well until you can handle your own.

**What the symbols mean (the key terms)**
These are the five labels, not maths symbols.

| Component | Plain meaning | Self or social |
|---|---|---|
| Self-awareness | know your own emotions and triggers | self |
| Self-regulation | control impulses; think before acting | self |
| Motivation | inner drive, optimism, resilience | self |
| Empathy | sense and share others' feelings | social |
| Social skills | build rapport, manage conflict | social |

**The formula or method**
Remember the group split as the method: first three = personal (handling me), last two = social (handling us). A simple hook is **"SSM then ES"** — Self-awareness, Self-regulation, Motivation, then Empathy, Social skills. When a question asks "which component is this?", first decide self or other: if the person is acting on their own feeling it is one of the first three; if they are reading or managing someone else it is empathy or social skills.

**Exam-level example**
"An officer catches himself about to send a furious email, realises it is wounded pride, deletes it, and rewrites it calmly next morning. Which two components combine?" Noticing the feeling and its source is **self-awareness**; deleting and choosing a calm reply is **self-regulation**. Empathy and social skills are about others, so they do not fit; motivation is about goal-drive, not this pause. Answer: self-awareness and self-regulation.

**Common traps**
- Listing "numerical aptitude" or "IQ" as a component — it is not; the five are only the emotional-social skills above.
- Mixing up empathy (reading others) with self-awareness (reading yourself).
- Forgetting that self-awareness must come before self-regulation.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation | the three self skills |
| empathy, social skills | the two social skills |
| self-awareness first | notice a feeling before you can manage it |
keyPoints: Goleman's five components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.
First three are personal (handling yourself); last two are social (handling relationships).
Self-awareness = noticing your own emotions/triggers; it must come before self-regulation.
Self-regulation = controlling impulses and thinking before acting; motivation = drive and resilience.
Empathy = sensing others' feelings; social skills = building rapport and resolving conflict.
items.mnemonic: Personal-then-social: 'SSM-ES' = Self-awareness, Self-regulation, Motivation (self) → Empathy, Social skills (others).
items.source: Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995) & Working with Emotional Intelligence (1998)

items.title: The Mayer-Salovey Four-Branch Ability Model
items.body:
### The Mayer-Salovey four-branch ability model

**The idea in one sentence**
Mayer and Salovey treat emotional intelligence as four mental abilities stacked from the simplest to the hardest: first you perceive emotions, then use them, then understand them, then manage them.

**Do it the slow way first (reason through a scenario)**
Watch a chairperson handle one difficult emotion and climb the four steps in order.
1. She sees a member's jaw tighten and voice sharpen and thinks, "he is angry." Simply detecting the emotion is **perceiving** — the most basic step.
2. She lets that read of the room sharpen her focus and decides this needs careful handling now. Letting emotion guide her thinking is **using (facilitating)**.
3. She works out *why*: he is angry because he feels overlooked, and that anger may cool into cooperation if he is heard. Grasping the cause and the likely change is **understanding**.
4. She invites him to speak first, acknowledges the point, and steers the room back to calm. Actively steering the feeling in herself and others is **managing** — the hardest step.
Done slowly, the ladder is obvious: you cannot manage a feeling you never noticed, so perceiving sits at the bottom and managing at the top.

**What the symbols mean (the key terms)**
No maths symbols — just the four branch names and the model type.

| Branch | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Perceiving | detect emotions in faces, voices, yourself |
| Using (facilitating) | let emotion aid thinking and problem-solving |
| Understanding | grasp emotional causes, blends and changes |
| Managing | regulate emotions in yourself and others |

**The formula or method**
The method is to recall the order and the model type together. Order, basic to complex: **Perceive → Use → Understand → Manage**. A hook is **"PUUM"**. Model type: this is an **ability** model, tested by a performance test called the **MSCEIT**, which contrasts with Goleman's and Bar-On's **mixed** models that fold in personality traits. If a question lists "managing" first, it is reversed and wrong.

**Exam-level example**
"Arrange the Mayer-Salovey branches from most basic to most complex." The right sequence is Perceiving, then Using/facilitating, then Understanding, then Managing. Any option that opens with Managing or Understanding breaks the ladder, because you must notice an emotion (perceive) before you can steer it (manage). Checking against the scenario above confirms the climb from step 1 to step 4.

**Common traps**
- Reversing the order and putting Managing first — managing is the top, not the base.
- Slipping "Understanding" ahead of "Using" — using/facilitating comes third-from-top, before understanding? No: order is Perceive, Use, Understand, Manage, so Using comes before Understanding.
- Calling it a mixed model — it is an ability model (MSCEIT); Goleman and Bar-On gave mixed models.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| Perceive → Use → Understand → Manage | basic to complex order |
| ability model, MSCEIT test | measured by performance, not self-report |
| mixed model = Goleman, Bar-On | blends abilities with personality traits |
keyPoints: Mayer-Salovey four branches, basic to complex: Perceiving, Using/facilitating, Understanding, Managing.
Perceiving (detect emotions) is the most basic; managing (regulate emotions) is the most complex.
It is an ABILITY model, measured by a performance test (MSCEIT).
Goleman's and Bar-On's approaches are MIXED models, blending abilities with personality traits.
You must perceive a feeling before you can manage it, which fixes the order.
items.source: Mayer, Salovey & Caruso — four-branch ability model

items.title: Cracking EI Scenario Questions (Administrator Dilemmas)
items.body:
### Cracking EI scenario questions (administrator dilemmas)

**The idea in one sentence**
In an EI situation question, the best option is almost always the one that stays calm, acknowledges the feeling, checks the facts, and then acts fairly — handling both the emotion and the task.

**Do it the slow way first (reason through a scenario)**
"An angry citizen storms in shouting that his pension file has been stuck for months. What should the officer do first?" Test each option by hand.
1. "Warn him that shouting will get his file rejected." This is a threat; it fails self-regulation and inflames him, so reject it.
2. "Call security to remove him." This treats a genuine grievance as a security problem and ignores the real delay, so reject it.
3. "Tell him to put it in writing and come back later." This is a brush-off that delays redress and raises his anger, so reject it.
4. "Listen without interrupting, acknowledge his frustration, and promise to check the status now." This calms the emotion first and then moves toward the fact-based solution.
Only option 4 survives, because it is the only one that lowers the feeling AND addresses the work. Doing this elimination slowly is the whole skill: knock out the aggressive option, the avoidant option, and the over-reaction, and the balanced option is what remains.

**What the symbols mean (the key terms)**
No symbols — these are the response types the options are built from.

| Response type | What it looks like | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Aggressive / impulsive | threaten, shout, publicly rebuke | wrong (fails self-regulation) |
| Passive / avoidant | ignore it, say nothing, pass the file on | wrong (fails ownership) |
| Over-reaction | drastic punishment or transfer that dodges the issue | wrong (disproportionate) |
| Balanced | calm, acknowledge, verify, act fairly | correct |

**The formula or method**
Use a four-word filter you can run in seconds, the method known as **CAVA — Calm, Acknowledge, Verify, Act fairly**. Steps: (1) delete any option that shows anger, threat or ego; (2) delete any option that avoids or dumps the problem; (3) delete any option that over-punishes or over-corrects; (4) keep the option that stays composed, names the other person's feeling, confirms the facts, and then solves it proportionately.

**Exam-level example**
"A normally punctual subordinate starts missing deadlines and seems withdrawn; you learn his parent is seriously ill. Best response?" Run CAVA. A formal warning is aggressive and ignores context; reassigning all his work without asking removes his agency; saying nothing is passive neglect. The option that acknowledges his situation privately and works out a fair, temporary adjustment both respects the feeling and protects the work — so it wins.

**Common traps**
- A "confident, firm" option that is really ego-driven or punitive — strong tone is not the same as emotional intelligence.
- A "kind" option that silently strips the person's responsibility or agency — compassion must keep accountability.
- An option that fixes the task but ignores the emotion, or soothes the emotion but ignores the task — the best answer does both.

**TL;DR**
| What you write | In plain words |
|---|---|
| CAVA | Calm, Acknowledge, Verify, Act fairly |
| cut aggressive and passive options | they fail control or ownership |
| cut the over-reaction | punishment that dodges the real issue |
| keep the balanced option | handles the feeling and the task |
keyPoints: In EI scenarios, eliminate aggressive/impulsive options, then passive/avoidant options, then over-reactions.
Winning method CAVA: stay Calm, Acknowledge the feeling, Verify the facts, Act fairly.
Beware 'confident' options that are really ego-driven, and 'kind' options that remove a person's agency.
The best answer handles both the task and the emotion, proportionately and fairly.
items.mnemonic: CAVA — Calm, Acknowledge, Verify, Act fairly.
items.source: Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); local APPSC GK PDF — Verbal Reasoning: Emotional Intelligence
